Oportet eum qui rector

[unclear] in speech. Do not be slothful and sluggish, nor given over to the sleep of idleness, but continually kindled in the fervor of the Holy Spirit. Do not neglect frugal hospitality; assist poor strangers mercifully with what diligence you can, knowing that this is proper to a priest: to have care for the needy. Have gold not so that you may keep it, but so that you may spend it in alms for the poor. Let the bellies of the hungry poor praise you, not the banquets of belching rich men. Let your table be with the poor and needy, because in such persons Christ is received and the heavenly court is honored. Avoid the banquets of proud rich men, especially of the powerful, in which nothing is done concerning the salvation of souls and nothing at all is discussed concerning spiritual conduct. Let your clothing be respectable, not costly. In giving alms do not seek glory from men, but expect praise and reward from God alone.

Be a father of the poor and protector of orphans. Let no poor man depart from you without consolation. Do not be a striker or quarrelsome among the people; injure no one wrongfully, but do good to all, so far as you are able, even to enemies. Never [flatter?] sinners, but rebuke them as one who has obtained authority from God. Do not be a striker of the consciences of the people entrusted to you, nor utter the word of God indiscreetly, but with the moderation of piety. Be merciful to penitents, and do not break the bruised reed, knowing that you have undertaken the care of the weak, not of the strong. For it is better to send the penitent with kindness to purgatory than, by the austerity of the confessor, to consign him in despair to hell. Do not neglect to pray your canonical hours with reverence and devotion at the times appointed by the Church. Likewise, do not omit to read the Hours of Blessed Mary ever Virgin, the vigils of the dead, with the other things due according to the priestly order. Have care for your household in the fear of God: if you have a family, persuade them by word and example to observe modesty and honorable conduct. Indeed, it damages the reputation of a priest among the people when the people speak ill of his household. Let your speech be strengthened by the testimony of the Scriptures, because whatever is taught apart from the holy Scriptures is despised with the same ease with which it is proved. I do not want you to imitate those who preach in the Church without learning, who frequently cite fables and phantoms of dreams, and are ignorant of the mysteries of the divine Scriptures. Ranting and garrulous priests, speaking without reason, do not edify the people, but labor to draw them into admiration of themselves by empty speeches and Aesopian fables. For it is a foolish and damnable abuse, with the Scriptures and the Gospel set aside, to teach the Christian people the fables of Aesop and the invented deeds of the Romans. And do not wonder if the unlearned people hear these things more willingly than the Scriptures, since you read that the Apostle foretold this. “There will be a time,” he says, “when they will not endure sound teaching, but according to their own desires they will heap up teachers for themselves, itching in their ears; and they will indeed turn their hearing away from the truth, and will be turned to fables.”

Hence Jerome says: To roll out words and, by speed of speaking, to create admiration for oneself among the ignorant crowd is the mark of unlearned men. A worn-out brow often interprets what it does not know, and when it has [unclear] its own things with others, it also claims for itself knowledge which it does not have. Nothing is so easy as to deceive the base and unlearned little crowd by fluency of tongue; whatever it does not understand, it admires the more. But you, speak the things that befit sound teaching, and do not seek the applause of the unskilled if you wish to find a place among the learned. Do not imprudently desire the care of souls, unless you have first learned, in accordance with ecclesiastical sanction, to govern yourself and others justly. For the office of teaching the people is subject to many dangers and is troubled by daily anxieties. For the ruler of souls must be without reproach, as a steward of God, not angry, not greedy for shameful gain, sober, just, kindly, embracing the faithful word which is according to doctrine, so that he may be able both to exhort in sound teaching and to refute those who contradict. he who has been appointed ruler of souls must teach no less by example than by speech. Indeed, even a robber can accuse avarice, but no one can amend it except one who does what he teaches. He is a delicate teacher who debates fasting with a full belly. Therefore life must be sought before doctrine, because one teaches more fully by deed than by speech. For the most excellent kind of teaching is the demonstration of example. And indeed the Lord Jesus first acted, afterward taught. For in teaching he uses the greatest authority whose speech is confirmed by the attestation of his work. The word of a ruler is easily carried out by subjects if it is supported by uprightness of conduct. But he who teaches well and lives badly destroys himself by the sentence of his own mouth, and does not turn his subjects away from bad instruction.

At the same time consider how dangerous the care of souls is, especially in these times, when iniquity abounds everywhere and the charity of many has grown cold. For the days are evil, and men are slow to justice, and the whole world is set in wickedness, and faith is rare on earth. Amid these things the word of God is despised by the people, the discipline of the Christian religion is neglected, priestly authority is scorned. Lay life, liable to many sins and crimes, neglects the remedies of penance, gives itself to deceits and frauds, and scorns the admonitions of priests. And unless the ruler of souls diligently announces to the people committed to him their crimes and the punishments owed to sinners, before God he too will be guilty of their blood. And after these things God will bring all things into judgment, where the shepherd of souls is compelled to render account for each one; if he has been negligent in this world, he is condemned more heavily. Therefore it is safer humbly to flee the care and rule of souls than arrogantly to usurp it.

For if each person scarcely suffices to render account of his own life in that dreadful judgment, how will he answer for so many thousands committed to him? O how well he lives who lives for himself. It seems good and pleasant among men for a bishop, abbot, pastor, or any prelate to live in this age; but who will be able to think how terrible is the end of the negligent man? For judgment most severe will be made upon those who preside, and the powerful will powerfully suffer torments. He passes well who lives simply, to whom no earthly honor is entrusted. For pastoral care is never without danger so long as one lives in this world. The greatest danger of all is when, the soul separated from the body by death, the earthly shepherd must be presented before the supreme Shepherd, God, to render account. Here now the moment of final condemnation is imminent, when an account of badly administered stewardship is demanded, and the blood of many sheep is required from the hand of one shepherd. What then will the unskilled shepherd be able to answer to the charges, he who was negligent in the care of the sheep? He must fall silent, because he has nothing to answer.

Therefore, brother, if you consider yourself fit for the care of souls, if you are preparing to rule the church of Mernice, know that you are to be brought into judgment for these things, and that according to the merit of your life you will receive glory or torment. But believe me: he dies secure who, putting aside care for others, lives for himself alone in the fear of God. For to whom much is entrusted, much also will be required of him. The priest, especially one having the care of souls, is God’s herald, so that he may announce to the people the will of the Almighty, and may heal those who sin against the law of the Lord by words of rebuke. Therefore he must be learned and most steadfast, lest either through ignorance he fail, or through inconstancy he fear the hatred of the perverse. For it is shameful, because of fear of the people, to keep silent the words of God. The priest must use a little wine, lest, if he gives himself to drinking-bouts, he become a reproach among the people. For the Apostle condemns drunken priests, and the old law forbids them access to the altar. In the Council of Agde too it is read thus: Before all things drunkenness is to be avoided by clerics, since it is the tinder and nurse of all vices. Therefore anyone who is proven to have been drunk, as his order permits, is either to be removed from communion for the space of thirty days, or subjected to corporal punishment. For wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness is insulting; everyone who is mixed up with these—

in these matters, he will not be wise. He who burns without wine with the heat of youth, and is inflamed by the warmth of the blood, if he is strong in body, should flee wine as poison, lest, suffocated by a manifold fire, he fall into the mire of lust. A stomach heated with wine stirs up lust, dulls perception, and weakens the head and the whole body. It is also said in a proverb: A fat belly begets a thin understanding.

Therefore, when you are invited and come to banquets of priests, do not forget clerical propriety, but be modest; beware lest either your tongue or your ears itch, that is, lest you either disparage others yourself or lend a hearing to those who disparage them. Know that all the things you say about others must be turned back upon yourself; perhaps you will be reproved in the very same matters that you were censuring in others. But perhaps you will say: I cannot do wrong to those who report it, because whoever plans to stop the mouths of everyone strives in vain; what, then, is another person's disparagement to me? Surely I cannot prevent people from speaking? But, as we said above, so present yourself before the disparager that he may learn to disparage no one, when he sees that you do not willingly listen to what he says. Do not associate with disparagers, says Solomon, because their destruction will come suddenly; and who knows the ruin of each? Namely, both of him who disparages and of him who lends his ear to the disparager. Be prudent in conduct, discreet in silence and taciturnity. Be diligent in examining the mysteries of the Scriptures, and if any matter of doubt occurs to you as you read, know that it must be referred to the interpretations of the elders. Nearby you have the school of the very ancient city of Trier, in which there is an abundance of learned men, to whom you will be able to have recourse in the uncertainty of questions. Let gold not be dearer to you than knowledge, because the fruit of wisdom is eternal, while the use of riches is brief and momentary. Let there be no one who prevents salutary study, not mother, not kinsman, not sister: do the work of an evangelist, learn what you are to teach, lest you prove to be an idol shepherd. You are one and have no second; for whom, then, would you heap up riches? Live temperately; marriages strip the mind of virtues and render the purse empty of coins. Buy for yourself, from the alms offered, codices of divine Scripture; taught by assiduous reading of them, you may worthily instruct the people committed to you and raise yourself by contemplation to heavenly things. Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and it will exalt you before God and men. Do not consent to the pleasures of the flesh, restrain the impulse of fury, and never forget death.

What Sort of Person a Priest Ought to Be in His Inner Conduct

Chapter Seven

Since, however, it is not enough for a minister of Christ to lead an honorable life before men, unless he strives to appear before God clean from every crime, I exhort you to direct your heart in the fear of the Almighty and never admit any thoughts against God. For it is necessary [unclear]

for a priest of God to be holy in mind and body, and clean in thought. Hence the Lord says: Be holy, for I am holy, the Lord your God, who sanctify you. And Peter the arch-apostle says: You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition, that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. Let charity hold first place in your heart, for it is the fullness of the law and the completion of the prophets. For the greatest of all virtues is charity, which consists in love of God and neighbor. God must be loved for his own sake with the whole heart, and one's neighbor for God's sake. But no one truly loves God if he hates his neighbor in the faith. For Christ is God and man. Therefore he does not love the whole Christ who hates man. No good work

God accepts [nothing] as good except what the flame of charity has kindled on the altar of the heart; for charity holds the primacy among all the virtues. Humility follows it, which is called the guardian of the virtues. Yet such is the eminence of this virtue that every other virtue quickly perishes unless it is strengthened by the foundation of humility. For the holy Pope Gregory says: “He who gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind. For by the very thing from which he is seen to carry something, he is the more grievously blinded.” Therefore the greatest adornment of a priest is charity, and the most precious pearl in his garment is humility. You too, brother, show forth these twin virtues in yourself, and you will be a fruitful preacher in the Church of God. Whatever you say, you will easily persuade your hearers, if you have charity in your heart and diligently show it in deed.

Let cursed ambition have no place in your heart; it so blinds the mind which it has once invaded that it brings forgetfulness of God and of one’s own salvation. Be a Christian lover of men and an enemy of vices. Keep the commandments of God, and do not neglect ecclesiastical sanctions. Honor all men for God’s sake; never consider anyone worthy of contempt. What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another. Let not the sun go down upon your anger. Flee the flatteries of the rich; never at any time stroke sinners. Deny yourself to your desires, so that you may become a disciple of Christ. Chastise your body, bringing it into servitude according to the Apostle; despise delicacies; love chaste fasting. Be compassionate toward the poor: feed the hungry, clothe the naked, visit the sick, free the captive, console the sorrowful, bury the dead. Do not love the world; do not seek riches; do not run after vanity. For no one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs. Do injury to no one, but learn patiently to bear injury inflicted on you, after the example of your Lord, who, hanging on the cross, prayed for his persecutors, that they might not perish. Have peace with all men, but concord and unanimity only with the devout. Do not be proud and arrogant, not given to wine and much eating, not a backbiter nor one who rashly judges anyone. Guard your actions at every hour, and let the memory of things to come always dwell in your thought. For Scripture says: “Son, remember your last things, and you will not sin forever.” Therefore always think that you are going to die; fear the day of judgment; dread the torments of hell. If you do these things, you will easily overcome all temptations of the flesh. Despise the pleasures of the world, so that you may be able to enter rejoicing into the joys of heavenly happiness. Do not deceive your soul: no one can rejoice here with the world and afterward reign with Christ. For through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God. Therefore, despising present things, let us hasten with every desire toward eternal joys. Guard your heart with every watchfulness, because life proceeds from it. If you have been overtaken by some fault, do not delay in seeking the remedies of penitence and cleansing yourself in confession through true contrition. Strive to enter into life by the narrow way, that is, not to fulfill the desires of the flesh, to hate the world, to live by the spirit. For serving God [unclear] against victory to rest, do not cease from the battle, because no one will be crowned unless he is victorious. But in this life there is no certain victory, but continual battle. He who has persevered to the end will be saved. A man will be proved at his end. The life of man upon earth is warfare. For you are a soldier of the highest King; it is not permitted you to abandon his contest. A good soldier follows his king wherever he goes. Where then is your King? In heaven. Why do you not follow him? What are you doing on earth, if you are a soldier of the heavenly King above? Why do you not follow your Lord? For he says: “If anyone ministers to me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also my minister shall be.” Let him follow, he says, not with steps of the feet, but with the paces of affections. The Apostle also says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself.” Therefore, just as those who serve an earthly king obey all his commands and, wherever they are sent, are ready and prompt, and no [unclear] of wife or

excusing themselves on the ground of children, so the soldier of Christ must obey his commands in all things, and in absolutely nothing excuse himself. You, therefore, who await the unfading crown of victory, labor like a good soldier of Jesus Christ; let no pleasure of the flesh touch your mind with its enticement. For nothing is happier than the soldier of Christ, to whom the kingdoms of heaven are promised; nothing more laborious, since daily he is in danger of his life; nothing stronger, which is overcome by the flesh. Let no house call you away, let no kinship hinder you, let no flesh constrain you. I want you to be without anxiety, so that you may freely think on the things that are God’s. Naked and unencumbered, fly to heaven, for naked your mother bore you, and naked the earth will receive you. Love that which [unclear]; seek that by which you may rejoice happily forever. Live so that you do not fear to die. A good conscience does not fear death, because it knows that through death it will come to the joys of the eternal heavenly homeland. You now have, most beloved brother, what you asked from me; you have some sort of rule of good conduct, to which you may conform yourself; you have a standard of holy exhortation, to which you may diligently have recourse. I have done what I could. For the rest, live according to the Gospel and the constitutions of the holy fathers, in which the whole form of Christian perfection is seen. Farewell, mindful of us.

From Spanheim, on the Kalends of April, in the year 1486.

Poem to the Clergy, exhorting them to purity of life.

1 Corinthians, chapter 3.

Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? But if anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him.

1 Corinthians, chapter 6.

Taking the members of Christ, then, shall I make them the members of a prostitute? God forbid.

Hear, sacred house of Melchizedek, order of priests, clergy sacred to God, company of the key-bearer of the starry pole. God has established you like a great radiance, and has given you to the peoples as a shining globe: that, irradiating the world with a bright lamp, you may dispel the darkness of the lands with light; that, pure, you may sacrifice to the terrible God, and give the sacraments with reverence to the nations purchased by crimson blood. You hold the seat of the Lord, you hold his throne, so that you may express the light of faith, which cannot deceive, and the law, in speech and conduct: as the sun makes the year fruitful with its rays, so may you make the world fertile with light. You hold exalted the royal glory of magnificent Jove, so that you may remember, by fruitful governance, to feed the nations, and bravely rescue those whom the adamantine bonds of the tempter hold entangled. God has anointed you with sacrificial oil, rendering you bright with every kind of gift. Since, therefore, you shine with manifold good, if perhaps you displease others, you do not displease me. But I would have you carefully warned, that you look into yourself and ponder well how much many things defile the sacred seat of the pontiffs and of the heavenly ones, and especially the foul filth of lusts. How displeasing it is, and how hateful, to the holy lover of virginal bloom, he cannot fail to know who unrolls the sacred Bible with vigilant care. Now therefore attend to my sad song. Since the purity of the flesh and the brightness of the mind, unstained, and chaste joys, ought to belong to the high servants of the prince and of God, why do I everywhere see so many little prostitutes now ruling over the clergy and priests? Why do I see men otherwise learned and celebrated, illustrious in riches and wisdom, so utterly losing their senses that they do everything at the whim of whores, and do not refuse to be ruled by a vile little woman? O royal seat of the Lord, you cherish very many in your gentle bosom, as a mother does, who allow themselves to be drawn by feminine enticements, like brute animals, to whatever impiety, disgrace, or crime. How vile a snare, how evil a servitude, when a wise man allows himself to be ruled by women’s counsels, at the whim of a harlot; and, shamefully forgetful of God and of himself, closes the way to fruitful admonitions. How blind, foolish, and miserable are all those who, bound in heart by tenacious snares, raise at home, with no small effort and expense, a pestilential serpent, indeed a perpetual evil more harmful than death. Unhappy clergy, open your eyes, so that at last you may see how grave a crime it is if you defile the temples of your flesh, consecrated to God, with the meretricious filth of the flesh, or if the mind burns with illicit fires. At least let some shame rebuke you, initiates

O initiates of the illustrious heavenly prince, let it not hereafter please you to submit your free neck to the services, command, and yoke of both a vile maidservant and a little prostitute.

If you count for nothing the laws of men, judgments, and threats, if finally you esteem reputation as worthless, let at least fear of perpetual fire draw you away from the foul fever of ancient lust.

“If anyone,” cries the Apostle, “has violated the temple of the Lord by forbidden intercourse,” if he has befouled the temples of his own flesh with the stains of prostitutes, the Lord God will destroy this sacrilegious man with grievous destruction.

Whom do the terrible threats not move, which the sacred volumes everywhere resound against the lovers of foul flesh? Or who would not call them foolish and stupid? Why, wretched man, do you weave snares for yourself, while you blindly love the present danger and do not fear the stern judgment of God?

Hardly ever will you set a limit to your crimes unless you flee far from the serpent’s breath. Who carries coals in his tunic and keeps it whole, or stands unharmed in the midst of fires? You cannot avoid the death-bearing plague unless, cutting away the root of the old evil, you drive out idleness, cups, and leisure.

What was stronger than fearsome Samson, who alone, with immense strength, was able to lay low a thousand men with a single jawbone? Yet a vile woman destroyed him, worn down, alas, by continual complaints. Therefore do not trust the tears of a wicked woman; let her prayers, together with her threats, be suspect to you. By its pestilential breath the flame of lust silently breaks into the inmost parts of the heart.

You should rightly shudder, recalling the crime of adultery in David, than whom scarcely anyone could be found more religious, not to mention his son, who in wisdom shone far beyond all other men. Yet both prudent Solomon and his excellent father were captured by women’s enticements; and by falling grievously do they not silently warn us to shun fierce dangers from afar?

You, therefore, who cast off all delays and shake out the death-bearing serpent, men, lest the Dragon hold you captive any longer: if the pestilential plague is unwilling to go out with gentle steps, drive it out of the house. Though, when driven out, she may cry out, murmur, [unclear], tearing reputation to pieces, pour forth insults against the house from every side, weep, and wail, let none of these things move manly hearts; they perish like the briefest smoke.

Rather, let terror, care, fear, and shame press your hearts with just dread and torment them, lest excessive [unclear] and the greatest punishment [come upon] you, when the spirit, filthy with many crimes, shall be set before the judgment of its Lord. Let not the cries, tears, reproaches, threats, and fury of a vile prostitute move you; but let the avenger of crimes, just and upright, terrify you, full of shameful deeds, and black Cocytian Orcus, and Acherontian Styx. Lest at some time, forgotten amid innumerable filths by the vows and goads of wicked Cypris, the avenging devouring flame of wickedness burn you, plunged utterly into the terrible lake, which always crackles with sulphur and fires.

Another Poem on the Dignity of Priests

Venerable men, priests of God, heralds of the Most High, lamps of the day, shining with the ray of charity and hope, receive with your ears the words of my mouth.

You serve in the sanctuary of God; beware lest you be barren or empty, if you wish to live with the true stock.

You are the protectors of the catholic law, the salt of the earth, the light of men, the shepherds of sheep, the walls of the House of Israel, correctors of morals, judges of the Church, teachers of the nations.

If the protection of the law falls, the law is abolished; if the salt has lost its savor, with what shall it be salted? Unless the light appears, the way will not be known; unless the shepherd keeps watch, the sheepfold will be broken into.

You have begun to tend the vineyard of God, which you ought to water with the streams of doctrine, to root out thorns and thistles far away, so that the roots of faith may be able to sprout.

You are oxen threshing on the threshing floor, prudently separating the grain from the chaff, the laypeople, who are frail and inconstant. Whatever laypeople see to displease you, they say without doubt is not permitted to them; whatever they see you fulfill in action, they believe is permitted and free from fault.

Since you have been established as shepherds of sheep, do not be idle like mute dogs. Sharp barkings are not lacking to you; the rapacious wolf envies the safety of the sheep. The flock

The faithful flock is sustained by threefold food: the Lord’s body, by which salvation is increased; the compendium of the word, which is to be given discreetly; worldly food, lest it fall into peril.

You are bound to preach the truth to them; but what, to whom, how, where, and when you must carefully reconsider, why, lest anyone say that you err in your office.

It belongs to the office of your dignity to give freely the gifts of grace to those who seek them; but if ever you sell the gifts of faith, know that you will incur the leprosy of Gehazi.

Administer the Eucharist freely to the people; hear confessions freely, baptize freely; according to the Apostle, give all things to all; preserve only that which is your own.

Let your conduct be religious, your conscience clean, your life virtuous, your habit regular, and your mind gracious; let no criminal stain defile you.

Let no pride oppress the sign of [unclear] mind; let your gaze be grave, let your habit be a witness; let nothing entangle you in dishonorable cares, you to whom the keys of the heavenly kingdom have been entrusted.

Be brief in speech, lest loquacity, nurse of vanities, draw you into guilt; let the word you set forth be shortened, for in much speaking sin is not lacking.

Be kindly, sober, prudent, just, chaste, simple, pious, patient, hospitable, humble, teaching your subjects, consoling the wretched, correcting the wicked.

Would that you could so bear the pastoral care and lead the spiritual life that, when you have put off the fleshly cloak, the Lord may clothe you with the eternal stole.

May he who sits on the throne of highest majesty purge you of vice, cleanse you from sins, come to your aid in your piety, so that at last you may sit in Abraham’s bosom. Amen.

Another.

A Poem on the Eyes.

From Lamentations, chapter 3.

“My eye has plundered my soul.”

If youthful strength is a care to you, if the welcome repose of a serene mind is so, with anxious zeal keep your wanton eyes safe everywhere.

Remember that, though they are small little eyes, they are the greatest enemies of the fragile mind; you must always restrain them with a bridle, unless you wish to perish.

For whoever delights to wander this way and does not know how to hold back his sight will feel great ruins of the soul, captive in love.

For Love, fearsome with his hidden bow, first striking the slippery little eyes, creeps into the veins and passes into the very ark of the heart.

The restless demon, ever watchful at the windows, keeps guard, and suddenly burns the mind with his breath if he sees the eyes badly at rest.

Therefore, whoever seeks eternal rest, fearing the fires of Gehenna, keep watch over the door; be ever vigilant in guarding your eyes.

What madness, evil as it is, compels you to see what it is not lawful for you to enjoy, and from which you feel the inmost parts of your heart wrapped in sudden darkness?

While you trust too much in yourself and do not diligently labor to cut away the causes of the disease, afflicted by a swift and willing wound, you burn wickedly.

Turning slippery images over in your mind, wretched man, you are burned within by a blind fire, cherishing a silent wound in your veins, by which you will perish.

Indeed, already you have perished before the Lord, burning violently with putrid heat, while in your madness you wickedly desire the crime and love the wound.

Why do you look with wandering eyes through all the streets at whatever comes in your way, when youthful heat burns even one unwilling more than enough?

The venom of the basilisk is less to be feared than deceptive beauty and an adorned woman: by sight the former kills the body, the latter the mind with everlasting death.

The prophet of the holy Lord is witness, the royal psalmist, who, seeing a woman’s naked body, suddenly fell into grave sin.

Who after this, I ask, will not fear for himself, when he sees that such a man fell? Whom will that pious David, made an adulterer, not terrify?

The End.

From what I have suffered I am warned to bear evils fittingly. He who profits others endures sharp goads here; thence [unclear]

The Vanity of All [unclear]

Donatus Faetius was printing at Brixen. In the year of the Lord 1577.

H Heinrich

Who after this, I ask, will not fear for himself, When he sees that such a man has fallen? Whom would not that pious David, Having become an adulterer, terrify?

END.

From the evils I have suffered I am admonished to bear misfortunes with composure. C.
